column2: Those deluded ones who slander Shiva-yogis fall, together with those who listen, into the hells until the destruction of the earth.

Only when there is a listener can there be a speaker of slander against yogis; therefore the listener is held by the great to be more sinful and deserving of punishment. But those who constantly serve Shiva-yogis with devotion
He should observe the steadiness of the mind and meditate on that again and again; they say meditation is at first with an object and then without an object.
obtain great enjoyments and in the end Shankara's yoga; therefore Shiva-yogis should be honoured by men seeking enjoyment,
with shelter, food, drink and the like, with beds, coverings and the rest. The dharma of yoga, being of the very essence, cannot be broken by the hammers of sin;
it should be known as like diamond grains; so yogis are not stained by sin nor by floods of affliction, as a lotus leaf by water.
The region in which a sage devoted to Shiva-yoga always dwells becomes purified; how much more is he himself pure!
Therefore the discerning man, giving up all other duties, should practise Shiva-yoga for the removal of all sorrow.
The yogi who has gained the fruit of perfected yoga may, for the good of the worlds, enjoy pleasures at will and wander here, or remain here.
Or, regarding sensual happiness as petty and giving it up through the yoga of dispassion, let him be freed of action at his own will.
The mortal who sees death approaching and ill omens abundantly should, devoted to beginning yoga, take refuge in a holy field of Shiva.
If that man, steadfast of mind, living there, gives up his life of his own accord, even without disease and the like —
whether by fasting, or offering his limbs into the Shiva fire, or casting his body into Shiva's holy waters by immersion —
The view of the good is that there is really no meditation without an object; for meditation is called a certain continuous flow of the intellect.
whoever gives up his life according to the rule stated in the Shiva shastra is liberated at once; there is no need to deliberate on this.
Or if one who has taken refuge in a holy field of Shiva dies helplessly through disease and the like, he too is thus liberated, without doubt.
For they praise death by fasting and the like as best, since it is done with a mind steadfast in trust in the shastra.
Whoever, having killed one devoted to reviling Shiva, or being tormented himself, gives up his life, so hard to give up, is not born again.
Whoever, unable to kill one devoted to reviling Shiva, dies himself, is liberated at once together with twenty-one generations of his family.
There is no man on the path of liberation equal to one who gives up his life for Shiva or for Shiva's devotees.
Therefore his liberation from the circle of worldly existence is swifter still. Having somehow resorted to one of these means,
or if one dies having duly received the purification of the six paths, the after-death rites should not be performed for him here as for bound souls,
nor should his sons and others especially observe impurity. For the sake of Shiva's conduct or Shiva's knowledge, one may bury his body in the earth or burn it with pure fire,
or cast it into Shiva's waters, or leave it like a log or clod. And if one wishes to perform a rite for him,
Therefore an intellect without object does not function here alone; therefore meditation with an object rests on the rays of the rising sun,

one should do only what is auspicious and satisfy devotees according to one's means. A Shaiva should take his wealth, if his descendants are Shaiva; if there are none, one should give it to Shiva; descendants who are bound souls should not receive it.
and that without object rests on the subtle; there is no other in truth. Or meditation with an object rests on a form with shape;
awareness of the formless self is held to be meditation without an object. That same meditation is called seedless and with seed,
by resting on the formless and by resting on form. Therefore, first practising meditation with an object and with seed,
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 40: the account of the journey of the sages of Naimisha. Suta said: Having thus told the sages, who had bowed to him, the yoga of knowledge that the Yadava had obtained from Upamanyu, who had conquered anger, Vayu, his self uplifted, vanished at once into the sky at evening.
Then Pashupata perfected ones, sages whose bodies were covered with ash, came in hundreds and merged into that radiance.
When those great-souled ascetics had thus merged, the radiance at once vanished; it was like a wonder.
Seeing that great marvel, the great sages of Naimisha, not knowing what it was, went to Brahma's forest.
Before their going, Pavana, the purifier of the world, had seen the Naimisha sages and conversed with those great souls;
then, having reported their pure understanding concerning Shiva with Amba and his attendants, and the completion of the long sacrificial session of the sacrificers
to Brahma, upholder of the worlds and source of the Veda, he was permitted to go about his own work and went to his own city.
Now Brahma, in his abode, was mediating between Tumburu and Narada, who were rivalling each other and disputing in song,
taking the middle ground amid the delights arising from the songs they brought forth, sitting at ease attended by gandharvas and apsarases.
Then, it being no proper time, the sages were stopped at the door by the doorkeepers and sat down beside it outside Brahma's palace.
Then Narada, having reached equality with Tumburu in song and been permitted by Brahma, the Supreme, to go with his companion,
Then at dawn the ascetics of Naimisha all rose up to perform the concluding bath at the end of the sacrificial session.
giving up their rivalry and reaching supreme friendship, surrounded by him, apsarases and gandharvas,
came out of the Creator's palace like the sun from a cloud, to play the vina before the god, the Lord Nakulishvara.
Seeing him, Narada, bull among sages, those of the six families bowed and asked with great respect about a chance to see Shambhu.
Saying, "This is indeed the moment; go in from here," he went on, intent on something else, in great haste.
Then those who stood at the door announced them to Brahma, and at that they entered the palace of the egg-born one in a body.
Entering, they bowed to the god from afar, prostrating on the ground like staffs; permitted by him, they surrounded him and stood near.
The lotus-seated one asked those standing there how they fared: "I know your story, since Vayu told it to us.
What did you do after the wind god vanished?" When the lord of gods had said this, the sages, after the concluding bath —
their going to the holy place of the Ganga, the pilgrimage to Varanasi, the sight there of the lingas installed by the lords of gods,
the single worship of the linga Avimukteshvara, the sight in the sky of that great mass of radiance,
Then, at Brahma's command, the goddess Sarasvati herself, gracious, flowed forth as an auspicious river of sweet water.
the merging of the sages there, then the withdrawal of the radiance, and their longing to know its true nature, which they had pondered themselves —
all this they told him in detail, bowing again and again. Having heard what the sages told, the four-faced maker of the universe
shook his head slightly and spoke in a deep voice: "The supreme success of the next world is drawing near to you.
By your long sacrificial session the Lord, long worshipped, has turned toward grace — this is indicated by what has happened.
What you saw shining in the sky at Varanasi was the supreme radiance of Maheshvara itself, called the linga.
The sages who merged there, keeping the Vedic Pashupata vow, became liberated, at ease, steadfast, their sins burned away.
That you too will soon attain liberation in the same way — this meaning is indicated by the radiance you saw.
The time for it has come to you of its own accord by fate. Go to the southern peak of Meru, frequented by the gods,
where my son Sanatkumara, the supreme sage, dwells, awaiting the coming of Nandi, lord of beings himself.
Long ago Sanatkumara too, though he saw the supreme Lord, thinking himself in ignorance the lord of all yogis, marred by lack of humility,
Seeing the river Sarasvati, the sages, delighted at heart, completed the session they had begun and bathed there.
very fearless, did not rise and do the other fitting things; then for that offence the angry Nandi made him a great camel.
Then after a long time, grieving for his sake, I worshipped the god and the Goddess and appeased Nandi,
and with effort his wretched state was somehow removed, and he was restored as before to his former youthfulness.
Then Mahadeva, as if smiling, said to the lord of ganas: 'The sage behaved so proudly, disregarding me myself.
Therefore you yourself, sinless one, tell him my true nature — the first-born son of Brahma, who thinks of me as if I were a fool.
I myself have given him to you as a disciple, to spread my knowledge; he will perform your consecration as overseer of dharma.'
Thus addressed, the foremost of all the hosts of beings accepted, bowing his head, what had once been commanded.
And so Sanatkumara, at my instruction, practises hard austerity on Meru to win the favour of this gana.
He is to be seen by you before his meeting with the lord of ganas; to show him favour, Nandi will soon come there."
Thus quickly instructed and sent off by the yogi of the universe, the sages went to Kumara's peak, south of Meru.
Then, having satisfied the gods and others with its auspicious waters and remembering what had happened before, they went toward Varanasi.
Then, seeing the Bhagirathi flowing south from the foot of the Himalaya and bathing there, they went on along its bank.
Then, reaching Varanasi, they were all delighted, and bathing in the Ganga where it flows north,
having seen and duly worshipped the linga Avimukteshvara, as they were about to depart, they saw shining in the sky
a divine and most wondrous radiance like ten million suns, pervading all the quarters with its own splendour.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 41: the description of the greatness of the Shiva Mahapurana. Suta said: There is a lake there called Skandasaras, like an ocean, its water sweet as nectar, cool, clear, deep and light,
by those plunging here and there into the water, standing on stones, with the remains of their offerings, with sesame, unbroken grains, flowers, and discarded darbha rings,
having completed the libations to the gods first, the sages in the middle and the ancestors, to the knowing brahmins who had come for the daily bath;
by those making worship on altars and the like, preceded by the sun's arghya, with many bali offerings and scattered flowers in place after place;
here with a leader of an elephant herd plunging, emerging and relaxing, there with does, deer and horses come to drink;
here with fine peacocks and elephants coming up after drinking, there bright with bulls and rival bulls butting the bank;
here with the calls of karandavas, there with the cries of cranes, here with the notes of chakravakas, there with the songs of bees —
as if speaking lovingly again and again with the various creatures that live on its wealth of trees, bathing, drinking and the like,
and with the cooing of throngs of cuckoos hidden in the tops of the trees on its banks, as if inviting day and night all who were struck by the heat.
On the northern shore of that lake, beneath a wish-granting tree, on an altar of diamond stone, on a soft deerskin,
Sanatkumara was seated, ever bearing a child's body, just then risen from samadhi, unmoving of self,
enclosed on all sides by heaps of crystal stones, covering every quarter with the blossoming flowers of all seasons,
attended by sages and honoured even by lords of yogis. The sages of Naimisha saw him and, bowing, came near.
While they were telling him, when he asked, the reason for their coming, a tumultuous sound of drums was heard in the sky.
At that moment a celestial chariot like the sun was seen, surrounded on all sides by countless lords of ganas,
crowded with hosts of apsarases, encircled by Rudra-maidens, resounding with mridangas and murajas, with the sounds of flutes and vinas,
rich with canopies of many-coloured jewels, shining with strings of pearls, surrounded by sages, siddhas, gandharvas, yakshas, charanas and kinnaras
dancing, singing and playing; with a banner bearing the emblem of the heroic bull on a staff of coral,
a banner worthy of honour, adorning its gateway. In the midst of that chariot, between two chowries,
beneath an umbrella with a jewelled handle, pure as the moon, seated on a divine lion throne with the goddess Suyasha,
by his splendour, his body and his three eyes, recalling the Lord to those who serve him,
as if the command of the maker of the world had come unbroken, as if Shambhu's grace to all stood there before them in person —
with moss, water-lilies, lotuses and night-lilies like stars, and waves like clouds, like the sky come down to earth,
the son of Shilada himself, bearing the glorious trident as his best weapon, overseer of the ganas of the lord of the universe, like a second lord of the universe,
able to restrain or favour even the creators of the universe, four-armed, noble of body, adorned with the crescent moon,
adorned with a serpent on his neck and the moon on his head, like lordship embodied, like power in action,
like nirvana fulfilled, like omniscience come together — seeing him, the son of Brahma, his face beaming, with the sages,
rose and stood with folded hands, as if offering himself to him. Then meanwhile, when the chariot had come down to earth,

he prostrated to the god like a staff, praised him and presented the sages: "These of the six families have long held a sacrificial session at Naimisha; directed by Brahma, they have come here out of longing."
Hearing the words of Brahma's son, Nandi, cutting their nooses at once with a glance, gave them the Shaiva dharma and the Lord's yoga of knowledge, and went back to the god's side.
And all that was told by Sanatkumara to Vyasa, my own guru; and it was told to me by the honoured Vyasa, and by me it has been told to you in brief.
This jewel of Puranas of the chastiser of the cities should not be told to those who do not know the Veda, nor to an undevoted disciple, nor to unbelievers; given out of delusion, it brings hell.
To those by whom it has been given, received, read or heard by the path followed with service, it surely gives happiness, the three aims headed by dharma, and in the end nirvana.
its eight quarters shining with lovely stairways and ghats of blue stone, easy to go down and come up;
You and I have done service to each other through the path of the Puranas; therefore I shall go, my desire fulfilled; may all be ever auspicious for us.

When Suta, having given his blessing, had gone, and the great sacrificial undertaking had ended, the virtuous sages, in the Kali age sullied by sense objects, made their dwelling in the environs of Varanasi.
And then, having kept the Pashupata vow in full with the desire to be freed from the noose of the bound, attaining all knowledge and samadhi, those blameless ones reached supreme peace.
Vyasa said: This beneficial Shiva Purana is complete; it should be read with care and respect, and likewise heard.
It should not be told to an unbeliever, to one without faith, to a deceiver, to one not devoted to Mahesha, nor to a hypocrite who flaunts dharma.
By hearing it even once, sin is reduced to ashes; the undevoted gains devotion, and the devotee shares in the increase of devotion.
On hearing it again, true devotion arises, and on hearing it once more, liberation; therefore those who seek liberation should hear it again and again.
Five recitations of this Purana should be made with a good mind; aiming at the supreme fruit, one obtains it, without doubt.
Ancient kings, brahmins and excellent vaishyas, by reciting it seven times, gained the vision of Shiva.
And whoever even now, devoted to devotion, hears this, enjoys all pleasures here and in the end attains liberation.
by those who had come down into it and those who had come up from it in numbers, bathed, with white sacred threads, white loincloths and bark garments,
This Shiva Purana is supremely dear to Shiva, gives enjoyment and liberation, is equal to the Veda, and increases devotion.
May Shankara, with his hosts, his sons and Amba, always bring welfare to the narrator and the listener of this Shiva Purana.
by young sages with matted locks, tufts or shaven heads, adorned with the tripundra, their faces smiling, helpless in their dispassion,
with pots, cups of lotus leaves, auspicious jars, water-pots and other vessels of the same kind,
with water being constantly brought, and flowers gathered, for oneself, for others and especially for the gods,
by sages of good conduct, grey with ash on their limbs, standing on stones in the water for fear of touching the lowly,
Giving up his own resolve, Jabali, devoted to the worship of Shiva, reached the world of Brahma in a very short time.
and they joyfully went to Himamshu, son of Soma. The other, supreme kala of Soma, remembered as the sixteenth,
abides in the moon for the deliverance of the ancestors. When Soma had gone into the plants, the milk of cows and the oblations,
and in the drinking of Soma at the great sacrifice, on the new-moon day of the dwellers in heaven — hearing that it had been drunk, all the asuras set out to drink up Himamshu.
For fear of the asuras, Himamshu took refuge on the Vindhya mountain. Hearing that he was in the mountain fortress, the asuras, out of their own fear, then
— when the sun had been seized by Rahu, O Bharata — the danavas headed by Kaya and Atikaya came against Himamshu.
All Rahu's brothers, the mighty sons of Simhika, seized Himamshu, those long-lived ones, for the sake of nectar,
and the wicked ones threw him down to the earth; then the gods cried out. Falling to the earth, Himamshu, delight of Soma, said:
May the god Ishana, terror of the danavas, protect me. Meanwhile, O king, for the protection of Himamshu,
a linga rose from the netherworld, radiant as the blazing fire of time; by that fierce arrow, with a roar of "Hum," the great asuras
were reduced to ashes right there by the god of gods, the trident-bearer. Then the god said to him: "Give up the fear arising from the asuras;
be devoted to Shiva and stay without fear, child." Then Soma went with the gods to Brahma's abode
and told what had happened. Then at his word all the deities headed by Brahma, led by Soma, went
to where Omkara stands on the bank of the Kalpaga, O Bharata. Seeing the god Tryambaka, who had destroyed the sixty,
the god Brahma, Grandsire of the worlds, spoke these words: "This glorious Himamshu, delight of Soma, whose form is nectar,
must be protected by you, lord, from fear of gods and danavas. The moon is declared the goal of the twenty-seven conjunctions;
you are the goal of all the worlds; therefore you should protect him." Hearing their words, Shiva replied as was fitting.
Having worshipped the lord of gods, Somanatha, lord of the world, named Pataleshvara, they all went to heaven.
From then on that place has been famed in the three worlds. Having bathed in the water of the Savitri pool, one should worship him;
for him there is no return — this is the truth spoken by Shiva. Whatever fruit there is in seeing the moon-crested one at Prabhasa, O king,
that fruit surely comes, tiger among kings, without doubt. Whoever lives there on alms until his time is past
has no return — I tell you this truly. By giving sesame water and by offering pindas, O Bharata,
one raises fallen creatures from hell, without doubt. By hearing and reciting this, one is honoured in the world of Soma.
With sacrifices, festivals and weddings, with Vedic blessings and auspicious rites, the four classes stood in their own dharma, and the other common people too;
the cow of plenty yielded desires, and the earth was rich in crops. That royal sage asked Vasishtha, most learned in Brahman,
as Shakra asks Angirasa, so did the lord of Ayodhya ask the family priest, the sole deliverer of the lines of Soma and Surya:
At what holy place shall I perform the great horse sacrifice? Tell me graciously, as you have seen and heard.
Vasishtha said: As the brahmin sages who know the Veda told you, O king, your sacrifice should be carried out by brahmins as officiating priests:
Marichi, Kashyapa, Angiras, Gautama, Durvasas, Chyavana, Dhumra and the great sage Kanva,
these and other lords of sages of praised vows, O king. The great king Indradyumna, lord of the earth, asked them:
At what holy place does a sacrifice performed give the fruit of desires and enjoyments? Tell me all this truly, eminent sages.
The sages said: Some say Varanasi, O king, and others Prayaga;
others the holy place Naimisha, others Pushkara; others Kubjamraka, others Gangadvara;
others Mayapuri, saluted by all the gods; others speak of Himasthana, Bilvaka and the Nila mountain;
others likewise Kushavarta and Rudra-Mahalaya, Ishana and Kedara — this auspicious one is all holy places in one;
others speak of Aurvatirtha, and Badarikashrama, Kalanjara, Nilakantha and Devadaruvana;
others Hemakuta, Virupaksha, Chandishvara, Bhuteshvara, Bhasmagatra, and Prabhasa with the moon-crested god.
These and other holy places have been told to you, sinless one; the various differing views of the sages have been declared.
Durvasas, as if laughing, spoke these words to the king: "Among brahmins seniority is by knowledge, among kshatriyas by valour,
among vaishyas by grain and wealth, among shudras by birth. While Markandeya is present, who has lived through seven kalpas,
who knows the truth of future and past, knows the three times and the three Vedas, knows the measure of Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesha, rich in austerity —
who else has the ability to speak of dharma and determine dharma? Go, great king, to Dharmaranya on the bank of the Kalpaga;
whatever Markandeya will tell, let the sacrifice be performed there." Indradyumna said: "As you say, divine sage, so shall I do, sinless one."
Having said this, to go with the sages to Markandeya's hermitage, the king spoke to the chamberlain Suvarchas
and to the minister Devagarbha, equal to Brihaspati: "Taking all the materials and implements of the sacrifice quickly,
come here, obedient to my command; with the brahmins who keep the sacred fires we shall go to the bank of the Kalpaga.
Let everything be prepared quickly so that the sacrifice may begin. Arrange separate conveyances for all these brahmins,
and arrange conveyances for the eight hundred queens. To the lords of the nine divisions of the earth, dwelling on the islands of the ocean,
to thousands of various kings, let the proclamation be made repeatedly: Chandradvipa, Setu, Tamrapatra, Shilashtaka,
Bhogadvipa, Saumya, Gandharva and Varuna, and the ninth called Kumarika — the nine divisions established.
Jambu, Shaka, Kusha, Krauncha, Shalmali, Plaksha and Pushkara are declared the seven continents; and learn of the oceans from me:
of salt, ghee, curd, milk, wine, sugarcane juice and water, the oceans like moats, declared as the measure of the earth.
The proclamation should be made to those who follow my command. Three hundred thousand milch cows with their calves,
a hundred and twenty-five thousand horses with dark ears, ten thousand elephants adorned with bells and ornaments,
four thousand vehicles that move at will, a hundred thousand young camels, gems and rubies,
fire-cleansed garments for the brahmins likewise, various foods and eatables and drinks of many kinds,
a hundred thousand workmen, and sesame, darbha and the like." Having commanded Devagarbha, the minister, the best of speakers,
mounted a divine conveyance with the brahmins there, filled with supreme joy, with his women and retinue,
and reached Dharmaranya, where the one who has lived through seven kalpas dwells. Seeing Omkara, the Kalpaga and the Vaidurya mountain,
Today I am freed from the sin committed even in seven births! — saying this he sat down, having prostrated with eight limbs,
and that best of kings duly worshipped the sage. Seeing the king, the great sage Markandeya said:
Are you well, tiger among kings? You are seen after a long time, man of good vows. What is the purpose of your coming with the brahmins and eminent sages?
Indradyumna said: "I have come to perform a sacrifice — at what holy place, best of brahmins? The Purana told you by Shiva, proclaimed by Skanda —
that I wish to hear: the great fruit of the field of sacrifice."
Markandeya said: Whatever holy places there are on the earth, reaching to the ocean's end,
come to bathe in the Narmada, lord of men. The lingas in the north and the holy places in the south
merge into the Koti tirthas; therefore it is remembered as Kotitirtha. It was told long ago by Shiva to Parvati and Shanmukha,
and declared to the gods Brahma, Vishnu and the rest, and to Shakra too; that I have told you, O king, as Shambhu indicated.
Near Omkara the Reva's Kotitirtha is proclaimed; whatever is given, offered or sacrificed here, or the hardest austerity practised,
has no end, as is the word of Maheshvara. At the conjunction of Rahu and Soma, Kurukshetra is praised,
but the Narmada gives merit always in all undertakings. Know it to be thirteen times greater, as the wise call the holy place;
they call Kotitirtha a hundred crore times greater.
Especially at eclipses of moon and sun, lord of men, sacrifice at the Koti tirthas, if you desire heaven.
Hearing his words, the supremely righteous king clasped there the feet of the sage of boundless radiance:
I regard what you have told me as a grace. Meanwhile, the sacrificial posts and implements having arrived,
kshatriyas of many lands, cows, horses and elephants — at once Devagarbha and the chamberlain handed them over.
Over thirty yojanas he made sacrificial posts and a pavilion, and fire-pits of various kinds to proper measure.
The roar of Vedic recitation touched heaven and earth; the fire became smokeless, radiant as ten million suns.
He invited Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra; the eleven Rudras were there, and the twelve Adityas,
the Vishvedevas, the Sadhyas, the Maruts and the Vasus, the eight world-guardians, the oceans and the rivers,
the trees, the mountains and holy places of many kinds, the guardians of the directions and of beings, siddhas, gandharvas and kinnaras,
all the Soma-drinking ancestors who give the fruit of enjoyment and liberation, rakshasas, guhyakas, bhutas and serpents as well,
the winds of the house and the dwellers in the sky, at the festival. Rivers flowing with ghee and milk, with mud of curd and sweet rice,
there were at that great festival of the king's sacrifice; and with foods and eatables of many kinds and desired conveyances and the like,
the gods, sages and the fourfold host of beings were satisfied. Thus the sacrifice was carried out by brahmins with abundant fees.
Then Indradyumna was praised by gods, asuras and divine beings; he assigned the shares of the sacrifice to the gods separately,
and the share of the Rudras as ordained by the Self-born. Yudhishthira said: Of the Rudras, Adityas and Vasus, and of the Vishvedevas who eat the oblations,
tell me the number, names and lineages, great sage. Markandeya said: Atri, Angirasa, Sarpi, Marut, Brihaspati,
Dhruva, Dhumra, Ketu, Dhara, Dhata and Hara — these are remembered as the eleven Rudras, all granting the fruit of desires.
Aryaman, Varuna, Indra, Pushan, Gabhastiman, and the one called Mitra, Jaghanya and Jalakrit,
Vivasvat, Parjanya and Dhata — these are remembered as the twelve; born in Kashyapa's hermitage, they arose as treasuries of radiance.
By the rule of the months they move at the will of the Supreme; all these day and night, and heaven all around.
Hear, great king, the eight Vasus as they are told: Dhruva, Dhara, Soma, Savitra, Anila, Anala,
Pratyusha and Kalpa — these are remembered as the eight Vasus. The sons of Vishva are proclaimed as the Vishvedevas:
Kratu, Daksha, Satya, Kala, Kama, Dhvani, Pururavas, Madrava and Rochamana — these are ten.
The sons of Muhurta are proclaimed as the Sadhya gods; and the Maruts are declared to be forty-nine.
The names of all these are well known, Yudhishthira. I have told you all that you asked me, sinless one.
Then, having dismissed Dhruva and the sages, the sons of Brahma, and then recognizing Omkara, the king performed worship.
He made ornaments for the linga with gems, rubies and jewels; with various fragrances and incense, camphor, aloe and sandal,
with banners, umbrellas and canopies, fans and divine chowries, having worshipped according to rule, he uttered this hymn to me:

On Omkara joined with the bindu yogis always meditate; granting desires and granting liberation — salutation again and again to Omkara.
skandapuran:34:82	Giver of boons to Brahma, Vishnu and Indra, all-god, salutation to you; to Kadruda, to Prachetas, to the thousand-eyed, to the bountiful.
skandapuran:34:83	Your auspicious form, Rudra, gentle and destroying sin; to you whose faces, heads and necks are everywhere, to the welfare of all beings,
skandapuran:34:84	the all-pervading Lord — salutation to him who goes everywhere. With hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads and faces on every side,
skandapuran:34:85	with ears on every side in the world, he stands enveloping all.
skandapuran:34:86	By the fickleness of my tongue you have been wearied, Maheshvara. This hymn to the god was made by Indradyumna, O Bharata.
In the midst of the linga a supreme linga, radiant as the blazing fire of time — what was seen spoke to the king, O Bharata:
Choose a boon — blessings on you — whatever is in your mind.
Indradyumna said: "If you are pleased with me, O God, and wish to give me a boon,
dwell here always, lord of gods, with Uma, worshipped in the divine valley, on the mountain of sacrifice.
Whoever gives up his life at this holy place, helplessly or of his own will, lord of the god of gods, let him go to Shiva's world.
One who has performed a thousand sacrifices, knows dharma and is lord of gifts and sacrifices, and the blind, dwarfs and men in animal births —
by death here let the two be equal, Maheshvara. Whoever encircles the mountain with a single thread on a festival day
has encircled the earth with its mountains, forests and woods; obtaining the fruit of all holy places, he goes to Shiva's world."
Omkara said: "All this, best of kings — let your desire be fulfilled."
Having said this, the god vanished right there; together with the gods, asuras, Adityas and Sadhyas, Yudhishthira, mounting his own vehicle he went to his abode on Kailasa.
The king too proclaimed to the fourfold host of beings: "By the power of my sacrifice, may all be free of disease;
may all be satisfied by the power of my sacrifice." Then Indradyumna praised Brahma, O Bharata.
Pleased, the Creator said to him: "Choose a boon, lord of the people." The king said: "If you are pleased with me, O God, and wish to give me a boon here,
bear the form of a linga on the southern bank of the Narmada; this I regard as the boon, if you are pleased with me, lord.
Let one who gives up his life there go to Brahma's world." "So be it, king of kings," Brahma said at once.
Having said this, Brahma went with the gods to Rudra's world. Then the king prostrated with eight limbs to Vishnu, Yudhishthira:
Hearing this hymn, the god bearing conch, discus and mace
spoke true words: "Choose a boon, lord of the people; I will give it to you, no doubt; you will attain the success of your sacrifice."
The king said: "On the northern side of Omkara, O Janardana, be in the form of a linga at the top of the Vaidurya peak, purifier of the world.
This I regard as the boon, if you wish to give it here. Those who worship here according to rule will go to Vishnu's abode;
men will not go to animal births nor to Yama's world; those who give up life there will go to that state.
By the gift of food to the ancestors, let the ancestors go to Vishnu's state by your grace — I speak the truth, the truth."
Hearing these words of the king of boundless radiance, Vishnu spoke to Indradyumna, lord of the people:
I will make an incarnation right here, best of kings; everything, best of kings, will come about by my grace.
Having said this, the god bearing conch, discus and mace went to heaven, praised by gods and asuras, O Bharata.
Thus I have told you, O king, of Indradyumna's great sacrifice; through it this holy mountain is renowned in all the worlds.
Know Siddheshvara as Brahma and as Narayana Hari; by hearing and reciting this, one is honoured in Vishnu's world.
Then the king, standing firm in his vow of truth, praised the holy places: "For the deliverance of the ancestors, salutation again and again to the holy places."
The holy places said: "Choose a boon, fortunate one, whatever is in your mind." Hearing the words of the holy places, Indradyumna said:
By my grace you must abide at the holy place near Omkara. Saying "So be it" to the king, they praised the river:

We bow to you, Kalpaga, supreme kala of Hara, best of rivers, exceedingly renowned on earth among all the worlds.

Then the best of kings, giving arghya, praised the Ganga: "Ganga, Bhagirathi, goddess, and auspicious Bhogavati,
Jahnavi, giver of liberation, blessed, deliverer, destroyer of sin, Mandakini in heaven, saluted by the god of gods,
you are Gayatri, mother of the Vedas, Uma and Katyayani; what more, goddess, since you are borne by Hara on his head?
Who but the one crowned with the half-moon has the power to praise you?" Ganga said: "I am pleased with you, great king; ask a boon, man of good vows."
Hearing the words of the Ganga, the king replied to her: "If you are pleased, queen of gods, and wish to give a boon here,
make your dwelling right here; let this boon be granted."
Ganga said: "So be it, king of kings; I shall flow here with a portion of myself."
Then the Ganga praised the Kalpaga, best of rivers: "You are the best, goddess Kalpaga, to be saluted, long-lived one.
By the power of your water purity has come to me. At the end of the kalpa, rivers, oceans and the rest perish,
and all the holy places; you alone remain here, worshipful and saluted by the gods, fortunate one, ever-flowing.
Equal to Gauri, you will be Hara's form at the tip of his matted locks." Having said this, the Ganga bowed to the Mekala,
and mounted a divine vehicle, praised by hosts of apsarases. Sarasvati said: "I am your daughter, protected by you in accordance with dharma.

and to bathe, goddess, after twenty-four years. Do you not know me, fortunate one, queen of the earth, flowing one?
